images.caption:
Hallsands
Original description:
Ruined cottages at Hall Sands, Stokenham

This does not seem a sensible place to build cottages, but they were originally protected by a shingle beach.  This was removed by the unscrupulous contractor for the Devonport Dockyard, who took away 500,000 tons of shingle. There were 37 fishermen's cottages, and they were demolished or damaged by a series of storms, the last cottage going in 1917.  This photo was taken in 1992, so there might be even less of the ruins now.

images.caption: Hallsands. Most of the village of Hallsands fell into the sea one stormy night in 1917. Remains of this lost village may still be seen at low tide. Royal Naval dredging was blamed for the tragedy and much of the coast is now protected with rip rap.

images.caption: Hallsands Bay. The village of Hallsands from near Start Point. Hallsands was a small fishing village that was destroyed by an easterly gale in 1917. The tragedy was made worse because previous removal of gravel from the bay had reduced the village's coastal defences. You can see the remains of some of the cottages on the left side.

images.caption:
Hallsands hotel-gone! Hallsands Hotel was demolished in December 2006. It is to be replaced by several 3 storey houses which will each go on the market for about £250,000. Erosion?
The houses behind the digger, are now inhabited by bats, so can't be demolished as the bats are protected.
The white buildings standing side on are four houses which were recently each sold for £27,000. There is a phenomenal vertical crack in the sea cliff below the houses, so who on earth has bought them?

The answer is that at least two were bought 20 or more years ago for peanuts with a council demolition order hanging over them, (subsequently cancelled). So they have served as cheap holiday homes for many years, and if they collapse into the sea in future years it will have been money well spent!

images.caption: The sea front at Exmouth, South Devon, England, looking west. This town is the westward end of the Dorset and East Devon World Heritage Site, extending 95 miles (155km) to Swanage in Dorset. The Heritage Site is also called the Jurassic Coast, although Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods are represented.
